cues.text: Arianism's Long Aftermath
The Council of Nicaea in 325 had condemned Arius, but it did not settle the Church's peace.

Successive emperors after Constantine tilted toward Arian or semi-Arian positions, and by mid-century the imperial Church of the East was largely in Arian hands, with pro-Nicene bishops such as Athanasius repeatedly deposed and exiled.
A related dispute also emerged over the divinity of the Holy Spirit .
A group called the Macedonians , or Pneumatomachi ("fighters against the Spirit"), accepted Nicene teaching on the Son.
They denied full divinity to the Holy Spirit, treating him as a creature subordinate to the Father and Son.
Throughout the middle decades of the fourth century, regional councils in both East and West produced competing creeds.
Each defined the relationship of Father and Son in slightly different terms, leaving ordinary Christians and many bishops uncertain which formula represented the authentic faith.
The theological work of the Cappadocian Fathers — Basil the Great, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa — refined the vocabulary of "one substance, three persons."
It finally gave the pro-Nicene party language precise enough to reunite around.
The accession of the emperor Theodosius I in 379 changed the political landscape decisively.

A committed Nicene Christian, Theodosius moved quickly to restore pro-Nicene bishops to the sees of the East and, in 380, issued the Edict of Thessalonica establishing Nicene Christianity as the empire's official religion.
The Council of 381

In May 381, Theodosius summoned bishops of the Eastern Church to Constantinople to confirm the Nicene faith, resolve rival claims to the see of Constantinople itself, and address the Macedonian controversy.

It was, at first, a regional council of the East rather than a summons to the whole Church; the West was not represented, and its ecumenical status was only recognized later, formally at Chalcedon in 451.
The council met in the church of Hagia Irene , one of the oldest churches in Constantinople, predating the famous Hagia Sophia.
Some 150 bishops favorable to Nicaea attended, along with 36 Macedonian bishops who withdrew early in the proceedings rather than accept the council's direction.
Meletius of Antioch presided until his death partway through the council.
He was succeeded by St. Gregory of Nazianzus , a gifted preacher and poet later honored as a Doctor of the Church.

After Gregory's own resignation amid disputes over his transfer from another see — a resignation he described with characteristic candor as a relief from the burdens of ecclesiastical politics — Nectarius of Constantinople succeeded him.
Completing the Creed

The council's central achievement was doctrinal: it reaffirmed the Nicene Creed against continuing Arian pressure and expanded its language on the Holy Spirit to close the door the Macedonians had tried to leave open.

The resulting text, traditionally known as the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed , confesses the Holy Spirit as "the Lord and Giver of Life, who proceeds from the Father, who together with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified."
This is the creed, not the shorter 325 text, that is recited at Mass today.
The council also settled the disputed succession to the see of Constantinople, confirming Nectarius.
It issued a canon granting Constantinople a place of honor "second after the Bishop of Rome"—a provision the West did not fully accept.
This was because it rested honor on political rather than apostolic grounds.
Reception and Recognition

Because the council had not been called with Western participation and Pope Damasus I had sent no legates, its decrees were not immediately treated in Rome as possessing ecumenical authority, even though the West welcomed its anti-Arian, anti-Macedonian theology.
Its expanded Creed nonetheless spread quickly through both East and West as the standard profession of Nicene faith.

Full ecumenical status was conferred retroactively seventy years later, when the Fathers of Chalcedon in 451 formally numbered it among the councils of the universal Church and had its Creed read into the acts alongside that of Nicaea.
Legacy
First Constantinople closed the theological argument Nicaea had left unfinished, giving the Holy Spirit's divinity the same conciliar clarity the Son's divinity had received in 325.

Together, the two councils produced the creed that Catholics, Orthodox, and most Protestants still profess as the fullest early summary of Trinitarian faith, making 381 one of the decisive hinge points in the development of Christian doctrine.
The council's disputed canon on Constantinople's rank also planted a seed that would grow into centuries of friction between the sees of Rome and Constantinople.

This friction concerned precedence and jurisdiction, running underneath much of the Church's later history in the East and never fully resolved before the eventual schism between Rome and the Byzantine Church.
